1.pericope_label: I will praise thee with my whole heart: before the gods will I sing praise unto thee... Yea, they shall sing in the ways of the Lord: for great is the glory of the Lord

schools.summary: Delitzsch treats the Greek ascriptions as evidence about the collection rather than the author, denies that anything favours David's hand while granting the speaker must be a king, and reads the psalm as composed out of David's soul — an echo of the promise in 2 Samuel — noting the contrast with the psalm before, where praise had to be dumb before the heathen and here the heathen kings sing it. Ellicott works the two cruxes: 'before the great or the mighty' for the gods, and the strain in the second verse, where one would expect the name magnified above the promise and the Greek and Latin wrote 'thy holy one' instead of 'thy word'.

Gill allows the reading of the preposition by which the kings sing of the ways of the Lord rather than in them. Calvin admits either sense of elohim and prefers the angels, on the ground that the solemn assembly is a heavenly theatre and that one purpose of the cherubim over the ark was to teach God's people that angels attend the worship of the sanctuary.

Clarke gathers the versional evidence at every turn — David in the Hebrew and all the versions, Haggai and Zechariah in the Greek and Arabic; the ark, the judges, the angels and kings for 'before the gods'; 'above all thy holy name' for the second verse — offers his own rendering where he can, judges the clause possibly corrupt, and rejects the use made of the angelic reading by those who would have angels carry our praises up to God. Wesley glosses the ways as God's counsel and gracious providences.

Henry reads 'before the gods' as princes and judges and great men in whose very presence David sang, and observes that praising God is work the greatest of men need not be ashamed of, since it is the work of angels and of heaven; on the second verse he takes the plain sense, that the judgments of God's mouth are magnified above those of his hand. Spurgeon notices that the psalmist never names the God he addresses, reads the gods as idols and refuses to stop singing before them, and finds a double wonder in kings walking and singing in the ways of the Lord.

Augustine begins from the word confess, and from the fact that this title tells only to whom the psalm is chanted, so that the first line must supply the subject. Confession in Scripture runs two ways, of sin and of praise: the first is so familiar that the hands hurry to the breast whenever the words are heard, but Christ, who was no sinner, said 'I confess to thee, Father' — and what follows shows it to be praise.

positions.summary: In the presence of Elohim, that is, before the ark where the sacred symbols of the Supreme Being stood — the versions offering variously the judges, the angels, and kings.
Before the great, or the mighty, as elsewhere in the Psalter.
Before princes, judges and great men, whether of David's own nation or visitors from others, in their very presence.
Before the angels, who attend the worship of the sanctuary — the assembly being a heavenly theatre, which is one reason the cherubim overshadowed the ark.
Before the idols of the neighbouring nations, whose worshippers would not approve the music and whose presence is no reason to suspend it.

debates.question: What does it mean that God has magnified his word above all his name?

positions.summary: That the judgments of God's mouth are magnified above those of his hand — the wonders of grace exceeding the wonders of nature, and revelation discovering more of God than reason does.

That the promise has been not merely fulfilled but more than fulfilled, the praise won going beyond what might have been expected — though one would expect the name to be magnified above the promise, and the Greek and Latin wrote 'thy holy one' rather than face the difficulty.
That God has magnified his name and his word on every occasion — all the versions reading 'above all thy holy name' — and that there may be some corruption in the clause.

debates.question: Do the kings of verse 5 walk in the ways of the Lord?

positions.summary: Yes, literally: here is a double wonder, kings in God's ways and kings singing there, converted as any other man is, by hearing.
No — it is against the parallelism to make heathen monarchs walk in righteousness; the preposition means they sing of the ways, compelled to acknowledge the glory of Jehovah.
They will admire the conduct and workings of providence even if they never unite with God's people.

outliers.summary: Turns on the angelic reading of 'before the gods', which has been alleged as proof that the angels present in Christian assemblies carry our prayers and praises before God: there is nothing like this in the text, since even granting that elohim means angels, the praise is neither offered to them nor entrusted to them.
Observes that in the psalm immediately before this one praise had to be dumb in the presence of the heathen, whereas here the heathen kings themselves are the singers.

themes: I will praise thee with my whole heart: before the gods will I sing praise unto thee.
I will worship toward thy holy temple, and praise thy name for thy lovingkindness and for thy truth: for thou hast magnified thy word above all thy name.
In the day when I cried thou answeredst me, and strengthenedst me with strength in my soul.
All the kings of the earth shall praise thee, O Lord, when they hear the words of thy mouth.
Yea, they shall sing in the ways of the Lord: for great is the glory of the Lord.

6.pericope_label: Though the Lord be high, yet hath he respect unto the lowly... thy mercy, O Lord, endureth for ever: forsake not the works of thine own hands

schools.summary: Ellicott draws the contrast out of the verb — from his exaltation Jehovah looks down on lowly and proud alike, but one look is a gracious interest while the other merely marks men as persons to be kept at a distance — quotes the maxim that lowliness and humility are the court dress of God, hears the twenty-third psalm behind verse 7, and on the last verse holds that the prayer's intention depends on the psalm's origin, rendering the final clause 'do not leave them unfinished'.

Gill presses that trouble is not an interruption of the way but the way itself, a road walked through to the kingdom, long but not endless; and reads the perfecting first of the kingdom God had begun to give David and then of the work of grace on the heart, which is gradual and certain to be completed.

Clarke keeps his notes short and firm — God beholds the proud at a distance and holds them in derision; experience of that mercy is warrant enough to trust it into any trouble — and refuses to narrow the last verse to one object, listing the body, the soul, the work begun in it, the work for Israel and the evangelising of the world as things God will not forsake. Wesley reads the same verse as the deliverance, advanced this far by no human help.

Henry has God, who needs none of his creatures, overlooking heaven and earth to cast a gracious look on the lowly while disowning the proud, passes on Hammond's suggestion that this is the sum of the gospel the kings will hear, and reads the promised hand as stretched not against the enemies but against their wrath, to set bounds to it. On the last verse he is careful about the order: the ground is God's everlasting mercy, and the confidence does not supersede prayer but quickens it. Spurgeon turns the verse into an exchange, and lists what God has refused.

debates.question: What is it that God will perfect?

positions.summary: First the kingdom — God had made David king over Judah and would finish by setting him over all the tribes — and then the work of grace begun on the heart.
Everything at once: the body, the soul, the work begun in the soul, the work on behalf of Israel, the evangelising of the world, the salvation of mankind.
Whatever is most needful, God knowing best what that is; and the ground of the confidence is not our strength but the everlasting mercy.
It depends on the psalm's origin: if it arose out of the troubles of rebuilding Jerusalem and reconstituting the state, the prayer is intelligible and expressive as it stands.
The great work of deliverance, advanced this far by no human help but by God's power and providence.

debates.question: What is the outstretched hand of verse 7 stretched against?

positions.summary: Not against the enemies to destroy them, but against the wrath of the enemies, to restrain it and set bounds to it, while the right hand does the saving.
Perhaps upon the wrath rather than against it.
Against the wrath of the enemies straightforwardly — God will quicken the sufferer though he were ready to die, and deliver him.

outliers.summary: Lists the offerings God has had no respect to — a Cain's sacrifice, a Pharaoh's promise, a Rabshakeh's threat, a Pharisee's prayer — and sets beside Nebuchadnezzar the men of his own century who boast of their culture and their freedom of thought and dare to criticise their Maker.

themes: Though the Lord be high, yet hath he respect unto the lowly: but the proud he knoweth afar off.
Though I walk in the midst of trouble, thou wilt revive me: thou shalt stretch forth thine hand against the wrath of mine enemies, and thy right hand shall save me.
The Lord will perfect that which concerneth me: thy mercy, O Lord, endureth for ever: forsake not the works of thine own hands.
